## Orthogonal Sets

:::{style="font-size: .5em"}

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
        A set of vectors \(\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\}\) in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is said to be an <b>orthogonal set</b> if each pair of distinct vectors from the set is orthogonal, i.e.,<br>

&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;&emsp;\(\mathbf{u}_i^\top \mathbf{u}_j = 0\;\;\mbox{whenever}\;i\neq j.\)
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```



__Example.__  Show that $\{\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2,\mathbf{u}_3\}$ is an orthogonal set, where

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},\;\;\mathbf{u}_2=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\\1\end{bmatrix},\;\;\mathbf{u}_3=\begin{bmatrix}-1/2\\-2\\7/2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

__Solution.__ Take the inner product of each pair of distinct vectors.

$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_2 &=& 3(-1) + 1(2) + 1(1)       &=& 0, \\
\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_3 &=& 3(-1/2) + 1(-2) + 1(7/2)  &=& 0, \\
\mathbf{u}_2^\top \mathbf{u}_3 &=& -1(-1/2) + 2(-2) + 1(7/2) &=& 0.
\end{eqnarray*}
$$

Each pair of distinct vectors is orthogonal, and so $\{\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2, \mathbf{u}_3\}$ is an orthogonal set.  

In three-space they describe three lines that we say are __mutually perpendicular.__
:::

## Orthogonal Basis

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
       An <b>orthogonal basis</b> for a subspace \(H\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a <em>basis</em> for \(H\) that is also an <em>orthogonal set</em>.
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

Consider,

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -1/2\\ 2\\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, 
\mathbf{u}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 8/3\\ 1/3\\ 2/3 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Since, $\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_2 = 0,$ they form an orthognal basis for subspace $W = \mbox{Span}\{\mathbf{u}_1,\mathbf{u}_2\}.$
:::

## Orthogonal Basis

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
To compute the coordinates of $\mathbf{y}$ in terms of basis $[\mathbf{y}]_\mathcal{B}$, we need to solve the linear system:

$$
c_1 \mathbf{u}_1 + c_2\mathbf{u}_2 + c_3\mathbf{u}_3 = \mathbf{y}
$$

or

$$
U\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{y}.
$$

In general, to solve the system we'd need to perform Gauss-Jordan Elimination that takes on the order of $n^3$ floating point operations.

<br>

However, in an orthogonal basis the coordinates of any point can be computed more efficiently.
:::

## Orthogonal Basis

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
        Let \(\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\}\) be an orthogonal basis for a subspace \(H\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).<br>For each \(\mathbf{y}\) in \(H\), the weights of the linear combination \(c_1\mathbf{u}_1 + \dots + c_p\mathbf{u}_p = \mathbf{y}\) are given by \(c_j = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_j}{\mathbf{u}_j^{\top} \mathbf{u}_j}\;\;\;j = 1,\dots,p\)

        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

__Proof.__  Let's consider the inner product of $\mathbf{y}$ and one of the $\mathbf{u}$ vectors --- say, $\mathbf{u}_1$.

The orthogonality of $\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\}$ means that

$$\begin{align*}
\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_1 &= (c_1\mathbf{u}_1 + c_1\mathbf{u}_2 + \dots + c_p\mathbf{u}_p)^\top \mathbf{u}_1 \\
&= c_1(\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_1).
\end{align*}
$$

Since $\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_1$ is not zero (why?), the equation above can be solved as $c_1 = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_1}{\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_1}$

To find any other $c_j,$ compute $\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_j$ and solve for $c_j$.

:::

## Orthogonal Basis

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
__Example.__  The set $S$ that we saw earlier, i.e.,

$$
\mathbf{u}_1 = \begin{bmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},\;\;\mathbf{u}_2=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\\1\end{bmatrix},\;\;\mathbf{u}_3=\begin{bmatrix}-1/2\\-2\\7/2\end{bmatrix},
$$

is an orthogonal basis for $\mathbb{R}^3.$

Let's express the vector $\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix}6\\1\\-8\end{bmatrix}$ as a linear combination of the vectors in $S.$

That is, find $\mathbf{y}$'s coordinates in the basis $S$ --- i.e., in the coordinate system $S$.
:::

## Orthogonal Basis

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
fig = ut.three_d_figure((8, 3), fig_desc = 'y in an orthogonal basis',
                        xmin = -3, xmax = 7, ymin = -5, ymax = 5, zmin = -8, zmax = 4, 
                        figsize = (6, 6), qr = qr_setting, equalAxes = False)
u1 = np.array([3, 1, 1])
u2 = np.array([-1, 2, 1])
u3 = np.array([-1/2, -2, 7/2])
origin = np.array([0, 0, 0])
#
fig.plotLine([origin, u1], 'r', '--')
fig.plotPoint(u1[0], u1[1], u1[2], 'r')
fig.text(u1[0]+.1, u1[1]+.1, u1[2]+.1, r'$\bf u_1$', 'u1', size=16, color='k')
#
fig.plotLine([origin, u2], 'r', '--')
fig.plotPoint(u2[0], u2[1], u2[2], 'r')
fig.text(u2[0]+.1, u2[1]+.1, u2[2]+.1, r'$\bf u_2$', 'u2', size=16, color='k')
#
fig.plotLine([origin, u3], 'r', '--')
fig.plotPoint(u3[0], u3[1], u3[2], 'r')
fig.text(u3[0]+.1, u3[1]+.1, u3[2]+.1, r'$\bf u_3$', 'u3', size=16, color = 'k')
#
fig.text(origin[0]-.45, origin[1]-.45, origin[2]-.45, r'$\bf 0$', 0, size = 16)
#
fig.plotPerpSym(origin, u1, u2, 0.5)
fig.plotPerpSym(origin, u3, u2, 0.5)
fig.plotPerpSym(origin, u3, u1, 0.5)
#
y = u1 - 2 * u2 - 2 * u3
# print(y)
fig.plotPoint(y[0], y[1], y[2], 'b')
fig.text(y[0]-2, y[1]+.1, y[2]+.1, r'$\bf y$ = (6, 1, -8)', 'y = (6, 1, -8)', size=16, color = 'b')
fig.text(y[0]-2, y[1]+.1, y[2]-2.5, r'${\bf y} = 1{\bf u}_1 -2 {\bf u}_2 -2 {\bf u}_3$', 'y = (6, 1, -8)', size=16, color = 'b')
#
fig.set_title(r'${\bf y}$ in an Orthogonal Basis', 'y in an Orthogonal Basis', size = 16)
```
:::


## Orthogonal Basis

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
__Solution.__  Compute

$$
\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_1 = 11,\;\;\;\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_2 = -12,\;\;\;\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_3 = -33,
$$

$$
\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_1 = 11,\;\;\;\mathbf{u}_2^\top \mathbf{u}_2 = 6,\;\;\;\mathbf{u}_3^\top \mathbf{u}_3 = 33/2
$$

So,

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathbf{y} &= \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_1}{\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_1}\mathbf{u}_1 + \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_2}{\mathbf{u}_2^\top \mathbf{u}_2}\mathbf{u}_2 + \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_3}{\mathbf{u}_3^\top \mathbf{u}_3}\mathbf{u}_3 \\
&= \left(\frac{11}{11}\right)\mathbf{u}_1 + \left(\frac{-12}{6}\right)\mathbf{u}_2 + \left(\frac{-33}{33/2}\right)\mathbf{u}_3 \\
&= \mathbf{u}_1 - 2\mathbf{u}_2 - 2 \mathbf{u}_3.
\end{align*}
$$

Hence, $[{\bf y}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}$.

:::

## Orthogonal Basis

:::{style="font-size:.8em"}

Finding the coordinates of $\mathbf{y}$ in the orthogonal basis is efficient because:

- There are $n$ inner products, each of which require $2n$ flops.

- Each coefficient $c_i$ can be found separately, so with enough computers available to work in parallel, you can perform the calculation in linear time.

:::

## Orthogonal Projection

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
A projection decomposes a vector into the sum of other vectors.

Suppose we start with two nonzero vectors $\mathbf{y}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$.

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ax = ut.plotSetup(-1,10,-1,4,(7,4))
ut.centerAxes(ax)
pt = [4., 3.]
plt.plot([0,pt[0]],[0,pt[1]],'b-',lw=2)
plt.plot([0,2*pt[0]],[0,0],'r-',lw=3)
ut.plotVec(ax,pt,'b')
u = np.array([pt[0],0])
ut.plotVec(ax,2*u)
ax.text(2*pt[0],-0.75,r'$\mathbf{u}$',size=20)
ax.text(pt[0]+0.1,pt[1]+0.2,r'$\mathbf{y}$',size=20);
```
:::

Our goal is to "decompose" $\mathbf{y}$ into the sum of two vectors $\mathbf{y} = \hat{\mathbf{y}} + \mathbf{z}$ such that

- $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is a multiple of $\mathbf{u}$: $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \alpha\mathbf{u}$ for some scalar $\alpha$. We call this the __orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $\mathbf{u}$.__

- $\mathbf{z}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$. We call this the __component of $\mathbf{y}$ orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}.$__
:::

## Orthogonal Projection

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
ax = ut.plotSetup(-1,10,-1,4,(9,6))
ut.centerAxes(ax)
pt = [4., 3.]
plt.plot([0,pt[0]],[0,pt[1]],'b-',lw=2)
plt.plot([pt[0],pt[0]],[0,pt[1]],'b--',lw=2)
plt.plot([0,pt[0]],[0,0],'r-',lw=3)
plt.plot([0,0],[0,pt[1]],'g-',lw=3)
ut.plotVec(ax,pt,'b')
u = np.array([pt[0],0])
v = [0,pt[1]]
ut.plotVec(ax,u)
ut.plotVec(ax,2*u)
ut.plotVec(ax,v,'g')
ax.text(pt[0],-0.75,r'${\bf \hat{y}}=\alpha{\bf u}$',size=20)
ax.text(2*pt[0],-0.75,r'$\mathbf{u}$',size=20)
ax.text(pt[0]+0.1,pt[1]+0.2,r'$\mathbf{y}$',size=20)
ax.text(0+0.1,pt[1]+0.2,r'$\mathbf{z}$',size=20)
ax.text(0+0.1,pt[1]+0.8,r'Component of $\mathbf{y}$ orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$',size=16)
ax.text(pt[0],-1.25,r'Orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto to $\mathbf{u}$',size=16);
perpline1, perpline2 = ut.perp_sym(np.array([0,0]), u, v, 0.5)
plt.plot(perpline1[0], perpline1[1], 'k', lw = 1)
plt.plot(perpline2[0], perpline2[1], 'k', lw = 1);
```
:::

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Note $\mathbf{y} - \alpha\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mathbf{z}.$ We want $\mathbf{z}$ to be orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}.$
:::

## Orthogonal Projection

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
Now $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{y} - \alpha{\mathbf{u}}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$ if and only if

$$
\begin{align*}
0 &= (\mathbf{y} - \alpha\mathbf{u})^\top \mathbf{u}\\
&= \mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u} - (\alpha\mathbf{u})^\top \mathbf{u} \\
&= \mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u} - \alpha(\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u})
\end{align*}
$$

Hence,  $\mathbf{z}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$ happens if and only if 

$$
\alpha = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u}}
$$

and since $\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \alpha\mathbf{u}$,

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}.
$$

:::

## Projections onto Subspaces

:::{style="font-size: .5em"}

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
ax = ut.plotSetup(-1,10,-1,4,(8,4))
ut.centerAxes(ax)
pt = [4., 3.]
plt.plot([0,pt[0]],[0,pt[1]],'b-',lw=2)
plt.plot([pt[0],pt[0]],[0,pt[1]],'b--',lw=2)
plt.plot([0,pt[0]],[0,0],'r-',lw=3)
plt.plot([0,0],[0,pt[1]],'g-',lw=3)
ut.plotVec(ax,pt,'b')
u = np.array([pt[0],0])
v = [0,pt[1]]
ut.plotVec(ax,u)
ut.plotVec(ax,2*u)
ut.plotVec(ax,v,'g')
ax.text(pt[0],-0.75,r'${\bf \hat{y}}=\alpha{\bf u}$',size=20)
ax.text(2*pt[0],-0.75,r'$\mathbf{u}$',size=20)
ax.text(pt[0]+0.1,pt[1]+0.2,r'$\mathbf{y}$',size=20)
ax.text(0+0.1,pt[1]+0.2,r'$\mathbf{z}$',size=20)
ax.text(0+0.1,pt[1]+0.8,r'Component of $\mathbf{y}$ orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$',size=16)
ax.text(pt[0],-1.25,r'Orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto to $\mathbf{u}$',size=16);
perpline1, perpline2 = ut.perp_sym(np.array([0,0]), u, v, 0.5)
plt.plot(perpline1[0], perpline1[1], 'k', lw = 1)
plt.plot(perpline2[0], perpline2[1], 'k', lw = 1);
```
:::

When calculating this projection, the direction of ${\bf u}$ is important but its magnitude is not.

- Geometrically: if we scale $\mathbf{u}$ by any amount, we do not change the location of $\hat{\mathbf{y}}.$

- Algebraically: replace $\mathbf{u}$ with $c\mathbf{u}$ and recompute $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$:
    $$
    \hat{\mathbf{y}} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^{\top} c\mathbf{u}}{c\mathbf{u}^{\top} c\mathbf{u}}c\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^{\top} \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top} \mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}.
    $$
:::

## Projections onto Subspaces

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
So, the projection of $\mathbf{y}$ is determined by the __subspace__ $L$ that is spanned by $\mathbf{u},$ the line through $\mathbf{u}$ and the origin.

<br>

Hence sometimes $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ is denoted by $\mbox{proj}_L \mathbf{y}$ and is called the __orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $L$.__

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \mbox{proj}_L \mathbf{y} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^{\top} \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top} \mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}.
$$
:::

## Projections onto Subspaces

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
__Example.__  Let $\mathbf{y} = \begin{bmatrix}7\\6\end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix}4\\2\end{bmatrix}.$  

Find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $\mathbf{u}.$  Then write $\mathbf{y}$ as the sum of two orthogonal vectors, one in Span$\{\mathbf{u}\}$, and one orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}.$

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
ax = ut.plotSetup(-3,11,-1,7,(8,6))
ut.centerAxes(ax)
plt.axis('equal')
u = np.array([4.,2])
y = np.array([7.,6])
yhat = (y.T.dot(u)/u.T.dot(u))*u
z = y-yhat
ut.plotLinEqn(1.,-2.,0.)
ut.plotVec(ax,u)
ut.plotVec(ax,z)
ut.plotVec(ax,y)
ut.plotVec(ax,yhat)
ax.text(u[0]+0.3,u[1]-0.5,r'$\mathbf{u}$',size=20)
ax.text(yhat[0]+0.3,yhat[1]-0.5,r'$\mathbf{\hat{y}}$',size=20)
ax.text(y[0],y[1]+0.8,r'$\mathbf{y}$',size=20)
ax.text(z[0]-2,z[1],r'$\mathbf{y - \hat{y}}$',size=20)
ax.text(10,4.5,r'$L = $Span$\{\mathbf{u}\}$',size=20)
perpline1, perpline2 = ut.perp_sym(yhat, y, np.array([0,0]), 0.75)
plt.plot(perpline1[0], perpline1[1], 'k', lw = 1)
plt.plot(perpline2[0], perpline2[1], 'k', lw = 1)
ax.plot([y[0],yhat[0]],[y[1],yhat[1]],'b--')
ax.plot([0,y[0]],[0,y[1]],'b-')
ax.plot([0,z[0]],[0,z[1]],'b-');
```
:::
:::

## Projections onto Subspaces

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
__Solution.__  Compute

$$
\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix}7&6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4\\2\end{bmatrix} = 40
$$

$$
\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix}4&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}4\\2\end{bmatrix} = 20
$$

The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto $\mathbf{u}$ is

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u}} \mathbf{u}
$$

$$
=\frac{40}{20}\mathbf{u} = 2\begin{bmatrix}4\\2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}8\\4\end{bmatrix}
$$

:::

## Projections onto Subspaces

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
And the component of $\mathbf{y}$ orthogonal to $\mathbf{u}$ is

$$
\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \begin{bmatrix}7\\6\end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix}8\\4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So 

$$
\begin{array}{ccccc}
\mathbf{y} &=& \hat{\mathbf{y}} &+& \mathbf{z} \\
\begin{bmatrix}7\\6\end{bmatrix} &=& \begin{bmatrix}8\\4\end{bmatrix} &+& \begin{bmatrix}-1\\2\end{bmatrix}
\end{array}
$$

<br>

Furthermore, $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ and $\mathbf{z}$ are orthogonal. We can quickly check this for ourselves using the inner product.

$$
\hat{\mathbf{y}}^\top \mathbf{z} = 8(-1) + 4(2) = -8 + 8 = 0.
$$
:::

## Two Important Properties of $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

**1.** _The closest point._

Recall from geometry that given a line and a point $P$, the closest point on the line to $P$ is given by the perpendicular from $P$ to the line.

So this gives an important interpretation of $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$: it is __the closest point to $\mathbf{y}$ in the subspace $L$.__

:::{.center-text}
```{python}
#
ax = ut.plotSetup(-3,11,-1,7,(6,4))
ut.centerAxes(ax)
plt.axis('equal')
u = np.array([4.,2])
y = np.array([7.,6])
yhat = (y.T.dot(u)/u.T.dot(u))*u
z = y-yhat
ut.plotLinEqn(1.,-2.,0.)
ut.plotVec(ax,u)
ut.plotVec(ax,z)
ut.plotVec(ax,y)
ut.plotVec(ax,yhat)
ax.text(u[0]+0.3,u[1]-0.5,r'$\mathbf{u}$',size=20)
ax.text(yhat[0]+0.3,yhat[1]-0.5,r'$\mathbf{\hat{y}}$',size=20)
ax.text(y[0],y[1]+0.8,r'$\mathbf{y}$',size=20)
ax.text(z[0]-2,z[1],r'$\mathbf{y - \hat{y}}$',size=20)
ax.text(10,4.5,r'$L = $Span$\{\mathbf{u}\}$',size=20)
perpline1, perpline2 = ut.perp_sym(yhat, y, np.array([0,0]), 0.75)
plt.plot(perpline1[0], perpline1[1], 'k', lw = 1)
plt.plot(perpline2[0], perpline2[1], 'k', lw = 1)
ax.plot([y[0],yhat[0]],[y[1],yhat[1]],'b--')
ax.plot([0,y[0]],[0,y[1]],'b-')
ax.plot([0,z[0]],[0,z[1]],'b-');
```
:::
:::

## Two Important Properties of $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
**2.** _The distance from $\mathbf{y}$ to $L$_

The distance from $\mathbf{y}$ to $L$ is the length of the perpendicular from $\mathbf{y}$ to its orthogonal projection on $L$, namely $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$.
    
This distance equals the length of $\mathbf{y} - \hat{\mathbf{y}}$, or in other words the norm of ${\bf z}$.

In the previous example, the distance is 

$$
\Vert\mathbf{y}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}\Vert = \Vert {\bf z} \Vert = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{5}.
$$

:::

## Projections onto Subspaces

:::{style="font-size:.6em"}
Let's combine two observations.

1. To decompose a vector $\mathbf{y}$ into a linear combination of vectors $\{\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_p\}$ in a orthogonal basis, we compute

    $$\begin{align*}
    \mathbf{y} &= c_1\mathbf{u}_1 + \dots + c_p\mathbf{u}_p\text{, where}\\
    c_j &= \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_j}{\mathbf{u}_j^\top \mathbf{u}_j}
    \end{align*}$$

2. The projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the subspace spanned by any $\mathbf{u}$ is

$$
\mbox{proj}_L \mathbf{y} = \frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}^\top \mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}.
$$

So a decomposition like $\mathbf{y} = c_1\mathbf{u}_1 + \dots + c_p\mathbf{u}_p$ is really decomposing $\mathbf{y}$ into __a sum of orthogonal projections onto one-dimensional subspaces.__

:::

## Projections onto Subspaces

:::{style="font-size:.6em"}
For example, let's look at $\mathbb{R}^2$, and suppose that we are given two orthogonal vectors $\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\mathbf{u}_2$, so together they span $\mathbb{R}^2.$

Then any $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^2$ can be written in the form

$$
\mathbf{y} = \underbrace{\frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_1}{\mathbf{u}_1^\top \mathbf{u}_1}\mathbf{u}_1}_{\text{projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the subspace spanned by $\mathbf{u}_1$}} + 
\underbrace{\frac{\mathbf{y}^\top \mathbf{u}_2}{\mathbf{u}_2^\top \mathbf{u}_2}\mathbf{u}_2}_{\text{projection of $\mathbf{y}$ onto the subspace spanned by $\mathbf{u}_2$}}
$$

So this equation expresses $\mathbf{y}$ as the sum of its projections onto the (orthogonal) axes determined by $\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\mathbf{u}_2$.

:::

## Projections onto Subspaces

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
Hence, coordinates are projections onto the axes!

:::{.center-text}
<img src="images/orthogonality/projection.jpeg" width=600 />

:::
:::

## Graham-Schmidt Orthogonalization{.really-smaller-title}

The __Gram-Schmidt process__ is an algorithm that transforms a basis $\{ {\bf v}_1, {\bf v}_2, \ldots, {\bf v}_n \}$ for subspace $H$ into an orthogonal basis $\{ {\bf u}_1, {\bf u}_2, \ldots, {\bf u}_n \}$ for the same subspace $H$. It operates as follows.

$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
{\bf u}_1 &=& {\bf v}_1 \\
{\bf u}_2 &=& {\bf v}_2 - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_1}({\bf v}_2) \\
{\bf u}_3 &=& {\bf v}_3 - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_1}({\bf v}_3) - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_2}({\bf v}_3) \\
&\vdots& \\
{\bf u}_n &=& {\bf v}_n - \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_i}({\bf v}_n)
\end{eqnarray*}
$$

In other words, we can find an orthogonal basis by iteratively removing the projections of all previous vectors, in order to keep only the component of each vector that is orthogonal to all vectors before it.

## Graham-Schmidt Orthogonalization{.really-smaller-title}

Here is another way to think about the Gram-Schmidt process.

- Set ${\bf u}_1 = {\bf v}_1$.
- Overwrite each of ${\bf v}_2, {\bf v}_3, \ldots, {\bf v}_n$ with the component of those vectors that are orthogonal to ${\bf u}_1$.
- At this point, ${\bf v}_2$ is now orthogonal to the subspace spanned by ${\bf u}_1$. So, set ${\bf u}_2 = {\bf v}_2$.
- Overwrite each of ${\bf v}_3, {\bf v}_4, \ldots, {\bf v}_n$ with the component of those vectors that are orthogonal to ${\bf u}_2$.
- At this point, ${\bf v}_3$ is now orthogonal to the subspace spanned by ${\bf u}_1$ and ${\bf u}_2$. So, set ${\bf u}_3 = {\bf v}_3$.
- Overwrite each of ${\bf v}_4, {\bf v}_5, \ldots, {\bf v}_n$ with the component of those vectors that are orthogonal to ${\bf u}_3$.
- $\ldots$

## Graham-Schmidt Orthogonalization{.really-smaller-title}

**Example.** Apply the Gram-Schmidt process to the following three vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ to produce an orthogonal set.

$$
{\bf v_1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \qquad 
{\bf v_2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \qquad 
{\bf v_3} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Note that these vectors $\{ {\bf v_1}, {\bf v_2}, {\bf v_3} \}$ do not form an orthogonal set. For example, ${\bf v}_{\bf 1}^\top {\bf v_2} = 1$, not zero.

## Graham-Schmidt Orthogonalization{.really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: .7em"}
The first step of the Gram-Schmidt process is simple:${\bf u_1} = {\bf v_1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$

Next, we need to calculate only the part of ${\bf v_2}$ that is orthogonal to ${\bf u_1}$.

$$
\begin{align*}
{\bf u_2} &= {\bf v_2} - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u_1}}({\bf v_2}) \\
&= {\bf v_2} - \left(\frac{{\bf v_2}^\top {\bf u_1}}{{\bf u_1}^\top {\bf u_1}}\right) {\bf u_1} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{1}{2} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ -1/2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}
$$

This process guarantees that ${\bf u_2}$ is orthogonal to ${\bf u_1}$. We can check this for ourselves.

$$
{\bf u}_{\bf 1}^\top {\bf u_2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}  \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ -1/2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = 1/2 - 1/2 + 0 = 0.
$$
:::

## Graham-Schmidt Orthogonalization{.really-smaller-title}

Finally, we calculate $\bf{u_3}$

$$
\begin{align*}
{\bf u}_3 &= {\bf v}_3 - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_1}({\bf v}_3) - \mbox{proj}_{{\bf u}_2}({\bf v}_3) \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{{\bf v_3}^\top {\bf u_1}}{{\bf u_1}^\top {\bf u_1}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{{\bf v_3}^\top {\bf u_2}}{{\bf u_2}^\top {\bf u_2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ -1/2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{1}{2} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} - \frac{1/2}{3/2} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} 1/2 \\ -1/2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} -2/3 \\ 2/3 \\ 2/3 \end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}
$$

## Graham-Schmidt Orthogonalization{.really-smaller-title}

It is not difficult to confirm that $\bar{u_3}$ is orthogonal to $bar{u_2}$ and $\bar{u_1}$

Therefore, $\{ {\bf u_1}, {\bf u_2}, {\bf u_3} \}$ is an orthogonal set, as desired.

```{python}

    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
        If we apply Gram-Schmidt starting from a basis \(\{ {\bf v}_1, {\bf v}_2, \ldots, {\bf v}_n \}\) for subspace \(H\), then the resulting set \(\mathcal{B} = \{ {\bf u}_1, {\bf u}_2, \ldots, {\bf u}_n \}\) satisfies the following properties:
        <ol start=1>
        <li>The vectors in \(\mathcal{B}\) are orthogonal.</li>
        <li>\(\mathcal{B}\) spans the same subspace \(H\), and hence is a basis for \(H\).</li>
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
```
